Article Title: In 2024, a Greek woman crossed Nepal's Great Himalaya Trail on foot in 52 days, setting the fastest female time on the route
Article Text:
Asimina Inglezou crossed Nepal's Great Himalaya Trail on foot in 52 days

The race began in western Nepal

Participants navigated challenging Himalayan terrain

Inglezou became the first female finisher

The crossing involved significant elevation gain

The 2024 event attracted international competitors

What made the achievement notable

Guinness World Records confirms the female record

Greek endurance athlete Asimina Inglezou completed Nepal’s Great Himalaya Trail on foot in 52 days, 6 hours and 23 minutes in 2024, earning the Guinness World Records title for the fastest female completion of the route. She undertook the challenge as part of the 2024 Great Himal Race, a demanding west-to-east crossing of Nepal that began in Hilsa and finished in the Kanchenjunga region. The journey took her through remote Himalayan landscapes, steep mountain terrain and routes involving substantial elevation changes. The event required participants to maintain their progress over several weeks while navigating challenging conditions. Inglezou’s achievement placed her among the athletes who completed the demanding Himalayan crossing and made her the first woman to reach the finish during that edition of the race.Guinness World Records officially recognises Asimina Inglezou for the fastest completion of the Great Himalaya Trail on foot by a female. Her recorded time was 52 days, 6 hours and 23 minutes, with the achievement taking place in Nepal between 9 April and 31 May 2024. Inglezou completed the journey during the Great Himal Race, which brought together endurance athletes attempting to cross the country’s Himalayan region.The Guinness record identifies the specific category as a female achievement completed on foot. This distinction is important because the Great Himalaya Trail consists of a network of routes rather than one single, uniformly marked path. Inglezou’s record therefore relates to the official category and the conditions under which the crossing was completed.The 2024 Great Himal Race started in Hilsa, in western Nepal, and continued towards the Kanchenjunga region in the east. The event organiser, Les Chevaliers du Vent, described the route as covering approximately 1,602 kilometres, with around 90,310 metres of positive elevation gain and 88,817 metres of descent. The journey was designed as a west-to-east crossing through the Nepalese Himalayas, bringing participants across varied mountain environments. Competitors were given flexibility in choosing their routes, meaning that their individual journeys could differ in distance, elevation and the trails they followed. The route passed through remote regions and included sections where traditional mountain paths had been affected by road construction and changing local infrastructure.Unlike a conventional race that follows one fixed course, the Great Himal Race allowed participants to select routes through the Himalayan landscape. The organiser reported that competitors travelled through regions including Upper Dolpo, Dhorpatan, Upper Mustang and the Everest area, depending on their chosen paths. Some participants also crossed mountain passes above 5,000 metres, adding to the physical demands of the crossing. The combination of long distances, steep climbs and high-altitude terrain required competitors to manage their pace and make route decisions throughout the journey. The changing condition of the trails also created practical challenges. Participants had to adapt to the landscape while continuing towards the finish in the Kanchenjunga region. These conditions made navigation and sustained endurance important elements of the event.Inglezou was one of three women who began the 2024 Great Himal Race. She became the first female participant to reach the finish at the Kanchenjunga Base Camp region. Canadian runner Rachelle Komarnisky was also reported to have completed the full crossing on foot. The event organiser listed Inglezou’s racing time as 367 hours and 35 minutes, while Komarnisky recorded 393 hours and 46 minutes. These figures formed part of the event’s results, while Guinness World Records recorded Inglezou’s overall completion time as 52 days, 6 hours and 23 minutes. The difference reflects the way racing time and total elapsed time were reported. Inglezou’s achievement was subsequently recognised under the Guinness category for the fastest female completion of the Great Himalaya Trail on foot.The scale of the journey was measured not only by its distance but also by the amount of climbing and descending involved. According to the event organiser, participants faced more than 90,000 metres of positive elevation gain across the route. Repeated ascents and descents placed sustained demands on competitors, particularly when combined with high-altitude conditions and remote trails. The route’s flexibility meant that individual participants could experience different mountain passes and landscapes. Some sections required travel through areas where access to facilities and established infrastructure was limited. Competitors therefore had to manage their energy and progress over an extended period. Inglezou’s successful completion demonstrated the endurance required to maintain a long-distance journey across Nepal’s mountainous terrain.The Great Himal Race brought together participants from different countries and backgrounds in endurance sports. The organiser reported that 26 people initially intended to undertake the full crossing, while 22 eventually reached the Kanchenjunga Base Camp area. Thirteen participants were reported to have completed the high-Himalaya crossing on foot. The race included competitors who travelled through different routes and faced varying terrain along the way. Because participants had flexibility in route selection, the event did not involve identical experiences for every runner. The results reflected the challenges of completing the crossing, with competitors required to sustain their efforts over several weeks. Inglezou’s performance stood out within the female category, as she reached the finish first among the women taking part in that edition.Completing the Great Himalaya Trail requires prolonged physical effort, route planning and the ability to adapt to changing mountain conditions. The 2024 race combined long-distance travel with substantial elevation gain and high-altitude sections. Participants had to maintain progress while dealing with steep terrain and the practical challenges of crossing remote parts of Nepal. Inglezou completed the journey in more than 52 days, making the achievement an example of sustained endurance rather than a short-distance speed performance. Her record also came within a specific female category, which Guinness World Records officially recognised. The achievement highlights the difficulty of undertaking a long Himalayan crossing on foot, particularly when the route includes substantial climbs, descents and varying trail conditions.Guinness World Records lists Asimina Inglezou of Greece as the holder of the record for the fastest completion of the Great Himalaya Trail on foot by a female. Her official time was 52 days, 6 hours and 23 minutes, and the achievement took place in Nepal between 9 April and 31 May 2024. She completed the journey as part of the Great Himal Race, which crossed Nepal from Hilsa in the west towards the Kanchenjunga region in the east. The event’s route involved approximately 1,602 kilometres and significant elevation gain, according to its organiser. By reaching the finish during the 2024 race, Inglezou became the first female finisher and secured a Guinness World Records title for her performance across the Nepalese Himalayas.
Article Summary: Asimina Inglezou completed Nepal’s Great Himalaya Trail on foot in 52 days, 6 hours and 23 minutes in 2024. She undertook the challenge as part of the 2024 Great Himal Race, a demanding west-to-east crossing of Nepal. The journey took her through remote Himalayan landscapes, steep mountain terrain and routes involving substantial elevation changes. The event required participants to maintain their progress over several weeks while navigating challenging conditions.

Article Title: In 1957, a South American moth was released in the Caribbean to control prickly pear; by 1989 it had reached Florida and was attacking native and endangered cacti
Article Text:
According to scientists, the South American cactus moth primarily attacks Opuntia species, commonly known as prickly pear cactus. It can also occasionally affect Nopalea, Cylindropuntia and Consolea species.

From pest control to ecological threat

A threat to native cactus

Turning sterile moths into a control tool

Testing the strategy in the field

A pest once deliberately moved around the world to solve an agricultural problem has become a problem of its own. According to a report by the USDA’s principal scientific research agency ARS, the South American cactus moth was introduced to the Caribbean decades ago to control invasive prickly pear. After reaching Florida, it began spreading through the very cactus populations native to the southern United States and Mexico. Now, researchers with the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Agricultural Research Service are working to stop its advance using a biological control method that turns the moth's own reproductive cycle against it.According to the report, the story began with prickly pear, a cactus considered an invasive agricultural pest in Australia during the 19th century. The South American cactus moth was introduced there as a biological control agent, helping reduce the spread of the unwanted plants. The same strategy was later used in the Caribbean. In 1957, the moth was deliberately introduced to Nevis at the request of the local government to control invasive prickly pear. The moth subsequently spread to neighboring islands and eventually reached the Florida Keys in 1989. From there, it expanded along sections of the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.What had once been a useful tool for controlling prickly pear in places where the plant was invasive was now encountering native cactus populations.According to scientists, the South American cactus moth primarily attacks Opuntia species, commonly known as prickly pear cactus. It can also occasionally affect Nopalea, Cylindropuntia and Consolea species. The damage begins when female moths lay their eggs on the cactus. After hatching, the larvae feed together, boring into cactus pads and tunneling through their interiors. As the larvae hollow out the pads, the affected sections can eventually die, weakening or killing the plant.Prickly pear has ecological value beyond its appearance. The cacti provide habitat for wildlife and nesting animals, while their root systems can help limit erosion and their dense growth can provide wind protection. Some species are also cultivated as specialty food crops in the United States and Mexico.Researchers are now fighting the invasive moth with a technique known as the sterile insect technique, or SIT. Entomologist James Carpenter of the ARS Crop Protection and Management Research Unit in Tifton, Georgia, is working with colleagues to mass-produce the moth on an artificial diet. Male moths are then exposed to radiation that makes them sterile before being released into areas containing wild populations. The sterile males can still mate with wild females, but the resulting offspring are unable to reproduce. Over time, repeated releases can reduce the number of fertile insects in the population. The work involves researchers from ARS facilities in Georgia and Florida, other USDA agencies and Florida A&M University.The research team is evaluating the approach at three locations: Dauphin Island in Alabama, Okaloosa Island in Florida and St. George Island in Florida. Each site is being managed differently to help researchers measure the effects of the treatment. Dauphin Island is receiving sterile moths alongside a sanitation program, while Okaloosa Island is undergoing sanitation alone. St. George Island serves as an untreated comparison site. Sanitation involves finding and removing cactus pads containing moth larvae or pupae, as well as eliminating egg sticks. On Dauphin Island, combining sanitation with sterile insect releases has already reduced the cactus moth population to levels that are nearly undetectable, concludes the online report.Images Courtesy: ARS, USDA
Article Summary: The South American cactus moth was introduced to the Caribbean decades ago to control invasive prickly pear. After reaching Florida, it began spreading through the very cactus populations native to the southern United States and Mexico. Researchers are now fighting the invasive moth with a technique known as the sterile insect technique, or SIT. Male moths are exposed to radiation that makes them sterile before being released into areas containing wild populations. The sterile males can still mate with wild females, but the resulting offspring are unable to reproduce.

Article Title: A sea captain built this Nantucket house around 1834; after being moved and restored twice, the 7,000-plus-square-foot home that sold for $9.5 million is now listed for $32 million
Article Text:
After being moved and restored twice, the 7,000-plus-square-foot home that sold for $9.5 million is now listed for $32 million (Image Credit: Realtor.com)

Built for a Nantucket sea captain

The house was constructed around 1834 for George C. Gardner, a sea captain and descendant of Richard Gardner, one of Nantucket’s early English settlers (Image Credit: Realtor.com)

The house was moved and restored

Historic details meet modern living

Pool, guest cottage and Main Street setting

A historic Nantucket home with a past as remarkable as its architecture has returned to the luxury property market with a $32 million price tag. Built around 1834 for sea captain George C. Gardner, the Greek Revival house has survived decades of change, including a move to its current location and two major restoration efforts. The 7,000-plus-square-foot residence at 141 Main Street later sold for $9.5 million after its most recent restoration. Now, the George C. Gardner House combines its 19th-century character with modern interiors, a swimming pool and a three-bedroom guest cottage. The details were reported by Realtor.com.The house was constructed around 1834 for George C. Gardner, a sea captain and descendant of Richard Gardner, one of Nantucket’s early English settlers. Gardner made his fortune through whaling, an industry that shaped the island’s economy and identity during the 19th century. The home reflects the architectural character of that period. Its clapboard exterior features a five-bay facade, a columned portico and a widow’s walk, a rooftop platform traditionally associated with the wives of seafarers watching for ships returning from voyages.Gardner eventually shifted the original house into a carriage-house role after building a larger mansion closer to the road. The property’s story, however, was far from over.By the 1920s, the historic residence had fallen into disrepair. Gladys Wood later purchased it and moved the house to Main Street, where it remains today. She also hired architect Alfred Shurrocks to undertake its restoration. Shurrocks was working at the time on the restoration of the Jethro Coffin House, considered Nantucket’s oldest house.The property underwent another major revival in the early 2000s. Its owners brought in New York preservation specialist Joseph Pell Lombardi, who prepared specifications for conserving both the exterior and interior of the historic residence. That restoration was completed in 2005, after which the house was sold for $9.5 million. Its latest listing represents a substantial change in asking price, with the property now offered at $32 million.Despite its age, the home is designed for contemporary living. The original architectural character remains visible through features including a central hall, a turned staircase and fireplaces in the parlor, library and dining room. However, the interiors are more modern than strictly period in style. A contemporary kitchen connects with dining and sitting areas, while several living spaces provide room for entertaining.One distinctive feature is the double staircase leading from the sunroom into the garden, often referred to as “friendship stairs”. The formal dining room also pays tribute to the residence’s connection with its original sea captain owner. The main house spans more than 7,000 square feet and includes four en suite bedrooms with direct pool access. The entire third floor is dedicated to the primary suite, which includes an office and a private deck overlooking the gardens and a privately held unbuildable parcel beyond the property.The 0.56-acre property also includes a swimming pool positioned at the rear of the lot. The pool serves both the main residence and a three-bedroom guest cottage, giving the property additional space for visitors while maintaining separation from the main living areas. Its location adds another layer to the property’s appeal. The house sits on Nantucket’s Main Street, surrounded by the island’s historic architecture, restaurants, galleries and boutiques. The water is about 10 minutes away.Nantucket’s historic district encompasses the entire island and includes more than 800 pre-Civil War buildings, making the setting particularly significant for a property whose own history stretches back nearly two centuries. The George C. Gardner House therefore arrives on the market not simply as a large luxury residence, but as a piece of Nantucket history that has been moved, restored and adapted while retaining many of the architectural details associated with its 1830s origins.
Article Summary: The house was constructed around 1834 for George C. Gardner, a sea captain and descendant of Richard Gardner, one of Nantucket’s early English settlers. The Greek Revival house has survived decades of change, including a move to its current location and two major restoration efforts. The 7,000-plus-square-foot residence sold for $9.5 million in 2005.

Article Title: A Florida artist spent decades turning his property into a maze of sculptures, strange buildings and gardens; after years behind closed gates, his family is reopening the Warlock House Halloween tradi
Article Text:
The artist became known locally as the 'Warlock of Wesley Chapel' because of the distinctive property he created. (Photos: The Warlock House)

How Warlock House took shape

Lewis VanDercar spent decades filling his Florida property with sculptures, gardens, artwork and unusual buildings.

Halloween tradition returns

Statuary tours planned in October

Lewis VanDercar spent decades transforming his property in Wesley Chapel, Florida, into an unusual space filled with sculptures, artwork, gardens, unconventional buildings and other creations. It is now being reopened for the first time, reviving the property's Haloween tradition, Wesley Chapel Record reorted.The artist became known locally as the 'Warlock of Wesley Chapel' because of the distinctive property he created. His connection with Halloween also goes back to the 1970s, when he lived there with his family and neighbours were invited over for stories, costumes, tricks and treats.The Warlock Family Spookfest will be held on October 3 at The Warlock House Enchantment in Wesley Chapel. The family-friendly event will allow visitors to explore parts of the property while taking part in games, crafts, storytelling, live entertainment and other themed activities.The event is also bringing back a part of the Halloween tradition associated with VanDercar. Children attending the Spookfest will receive Warlock Apprentice Passports and can collect stamps at different themed stations. The activities include pirates, mermaids, herbology, bubbles, carnival games, broom decorating and storytelling.VanDercar moved to the Wesley Chapel area in 1973 and bought eight acres of land. He later built a dome-shaped, ivy-covered home that was designed to resemble a cave. Over the years, he filled the property with concrete sculptures, gardens, artwork and unusual architecture.His work was not limited to his own property. Before moving to Wesley Chapel, VanDercar drew Popeye cartoons from a Miami studio in the late 1930s. He later served in the merchant marines during World War II and worked as an aircraft engineer before making a living through painting and sculpting.Among his other works were a gorilla’s lair for Monkey Jungle in South Dade and a giant dragon for a park on Merritt Island.The unusual nature of his work also led to questions about whether he was a 'crazy' artist or a genius. In his December 1988 Miami Herald obituary, VanDercar responded to the description by saying, “I'm both. I think us geniuses should be modest.”The property he created eventually became closely associated with his identity as the 'Warlock of Wesley Chapel'. His grandson Bobby VanDercar now operates VanDercar Studio, a painting business in the Tampa area. The studio’s website describes Lewis VanDercar’s concrete sculptures as having transformed the Wesley Chapel property into an artistic landmark.According to the Wesley Chapel Record, a neighbour named Jeff Daniels recalled that VanDercar “would invite us neighbor kids over at Halloween to tell us stories.”The new Spookfest is built around a similar family-friendly approach. Rather than focusing on frightening visitors, the event will offer themed activities that children can explore around the property.Children will use their Warlock Apprentice Passports as they move between activities. They can collect stamps at the different stations and receive a special prize after completing their adventure.The event will also include games, crafts, live entertainment, food vendors and other activities. Families can attend in costumes, although the organisers describe the experience as playful rather than scary.According to The Laker Lutz News, the festival will take place from 2 to 6 pm. on October 3 at The Warlock House Enchantment, located at 25950 Queen Sago Place in Wesley Chapel.Admission is $15 for adults and $10 for children aged 10 and older. Children younger than 10 can attend for free.The Halloween event is not the only opportunity for people to see the property. The Warlock House Enchantment will also offer statuary tours on Tuesdays and Fridays throughout October.The tours are scheduled for 7 pm and 10 pm and will give visitors an opportunity to see the sculptures and other creations on the historic property.The opening marks a change for a place that had largely remained behind closed gates. Details about the Spookfest and October statuary tours are available through The Warlock House Enchantment.
Article Summary: The Warlock Family Spookfest will be held on October 3 at The Warlock House Enchantment in Wesley Chapel. The family-friendly event will allow visitors to explore parts of the property while taking part in games, crafts, storytelling, live entertainment and other themed activities.

Article Title: Hospital sent pregnant UK woman home, but hours later she gave birth in a KFC car park while rushing back; names her newborn ‘Colonel Cody’
Article Text:
Pic credit: Stephen Kirby/SWNS

Hours after being sent home, woman goes into labour on the A38

Pic credit: Stephen Kirby/SWNS

Giving birth in KFC’s car park

Pic credit: Stephen Kirby/SWNS

They named him Colonel Cody

Pic credit: Stephen Kirby/SWNS

A baby’s name is often chosen for its meaning, family history or cultural tradition. But for Katie Murphy, 33, and Stephen Kirby, 32, the choice came down to circumstance and a car park that would define their son’s entire origin story. Katie and her partner welcomed their son in unexpected circumstances, which prompted them to name him after KFC’s famous founder, Colonel Harland Sanders, news agency SWNS reported.It was August 29. Katie Murphy and her partner drove to the hospital early in the morning after she felt the baby was coming. The doctors examined her, told her everything was fine and sent her back home. The contractions had started before they left the hospital, intensifying during the thirty-minute drive back to Bromsgrove. “They got more intense when we were at home, but Katie didn’t want to go back to [the] hospital yet in case we were turned away,” Kirby told the outlet.Eight hours later, the contractions grew stronger. The couple had no choice but to head to the hospital again. “Finally, at around 9 p.m., she was in so much discomfort that we just said, ‘Let’s go,’ and I got her in a car to get to the hospital,” he said. “The drive is around half an hour, but around halfway through the journey, Katie said she could feel something and knew the baby was coming,” Kirby said.He was on the phone to get an ambulance. “They were asking what our location was, but we were on the A38, and there was nowhere to pull in.” The A38 traffic hummed around them, with no exits in sight.That’s when Kirby saw the KFC. Not a hospital, not an ambulance station, but a car park with pavement, light and witnesses. He knew this was their salvation. It was the KFC they frequented. He pulled in at 9:35 p.m. “Thankfully, I saw the KFC we often go to and pulled into the car park,” he said.As they pulled into the space, the woman could feel her baby’s head emerging. Kirby raced around to the passenger side, opened the door and caught their newborn before anything else happened. And there he was: a baby boy, born in a car in a fast-food car park. “When the ambulance dispatcher was trying to locate our location, the only place we could find was the KFC. As my partner pulled into the car park, and as he made his way round to the passenger side and opened the door, he caught my son just in time,” the new mum told the agency.The baby was in perfect health. The newborn weighed 7 lb, 8 oz. Now was the time to name the baby. They named him Cody. But it came with a nickname: Colonel Cody, after KFC’s Colonel Harland Sanders.“We call him Colonel Cody, and I think that nickname will definitely stick with him for life,” the mother said.The fast-food restaurant chain was undoubtedly glad to hear the family nicknaming the baby after its founder. In a statement, a KFC spokesperson said, “We’re honoured to have been the place of Cody’s birth and are sending bucket loads of love to the whole family, along with some KFC merch and vouchers to help them celebrate. We can’t wait to welcome them back for a meal to mark the occasion.”The new parents are already planning his first birthday trip. Back to the same KFC; a homecoming of sorts. There’s talk of a weekend job when he’s old enough, a joke that might not stay a joke. “We were famous amongst the midwifery staff, and they even ordered KFC for dinner. It was decided that we have to take him to KFC for his first birthday and get him his first weekend job there,” the mum said.Minutes after giving birth, the ambulance arrived and took the family to the hospital. “It all happened so fast. Thankfully, the ambulance was with us about five minutes later and took us to the hospital. Despite his abrupt entrance into the world in his dad’s car, Cody is in perfect health and is doing great,” the new mum recalled. The mother and the newborn got the medical attention they needed. And Cody’s unusual birth is a one-of-a-kind story that is sure to dominate family dinner conversations for years to come. “It was definitely not the birth I expected, but it was worth every bit of pain, and now he has a very weird story to tell his school friends when he grows up,” Katie Murphy said.
Article Summary: Katie Murphy, 33, and Stephen Kirby, 32, went to hospital on August 29. After being sent home, she went into labour hours later on the A38. The couple had no choice but to go back to the hospital, but the only place they could find was a KFC. As they pulled into the car park, the woman could feel her baby’s head emerging. Kirby raced around to the passenger side and caught their newborn.

Article Title: Einstein’s ‘spooky action’ survives one of the most extreme tests yet: CERN finds strong evidence that heavy Z bosons can become quantum-entangled
Article Text:
What exactly is ‘ spooky action ’?

Why Z bosons matter

The particles disappear almost instantly

An extreme new setting for quantum entanglement

Could it reveal new physics?

Einstein famously found quantum mechanics so strange that he once referred to quantum entanglement as “spooky action at a distance”. More than a century later, one of the strangest predictions of quantum theory has now been tested in an environment far removed from the relatively low-energy systems where entanglement is usually studied.Physicists working with the ATLAS and CMS experiments at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider (LHC) have found strong evidence that two extremely short-lived, massive particles known as Z bosons can become quantum-entangled. The result provides a new demonstration that quantum correlations can survive even at the extreme energies produced in particle collisions.The finding, reported by CERN in September 2026, involves Z bosons created when a Higgs boson decays. Researchers reconstructed the properties of the short-lived particles from what they left behind in the detectors and used statistical analysis to determine whether their behaviour was consistent with quantum entanglement.Quantum entanglement occurs when two quantum systems share a linked state, meaning measurements of one are correlated with measurements of the other in ways that cannot be explained by treating the particles as completely independent.This was one of the aspects of quantum mechanics that troubled Einstein and other physicists. They questioned whether particles might possess hidden properties that determined their behaviour before measurement, rather than nature genuinely following the unusual rules of quantum mechanics.Experiments over the decades have repeatedly supported quantum mechanics and demonstrated entanglement in different physical systems. What makes the latest CERN result notable is the extreme environment in which the effect was observed.The researchers were not watching two Z bosons sitting apart and exchanging information. Instead, they examined the quantum correlations encoded in particles produced together during a Higgs boson decay.The Z boson is one of the fundamental particles responsible for carrying the weak nuclear force, one of the four fundamental forces of nature. It is also extremely unstable, decaying almost immediately after being produced.That short lifetime means scientists cannot simply capture a Z boson and directly measure it later. Instead, they reconstruct what happened by studying its decay products.In this case, the researchers focused on Higgs boson decays in which a Higgs produces two Z bosons, written as H → ZZ*. The Z bosons subsequently decay into pairs of leptons, such as electrons or muons. Those particles can be detected by ATLAS and CMS, allowing scientists to work backwards and infer properties of the original Z bosons.The process is particularly useful because the Higgs boson has zero spin. Z bosons, meanwhile, can have three possible spin states: -1, 0 and +1.When two Z bosons are produced from a Higgs decay, their combined spin must be consistent with the Higgs boson's spin. This creates specific quantum correlations between them. Researchers can examine those correlations to determine whether the pair behaves as an entangled quantum system.One of the most unusual aspects of the experiment is that the Z bosons themselves do not survive long enough to be directly observed. Instead, ATLAS and CMS detected the electrons and muons produced by their decay. From the directions and other properties of these particles, researchers reconstructed information about the Z bosons' spins.They then analysed the resulting angular distributions and other observables statistically. The ATLAS measurement, published in Physical Review Letters on September 11, 2026, reported that a hypothesis assuming the two Z bosons were separable was disfavoured at a significance of 4.7 standard deviations relative to the entangled Standard Model hypothesis. The expected significance was 4.9 standard deviations.In particle physics, a result at this level is described as strong evidence, rather than the discovery standard of 5 standard deviations. The distinction matters because the measurement is based on statistical evidence and relies on several Standard Model assumptions in the decay analysis.Quantum entanglement has previously been observed in many different systems, but most demonstrations have involved relatively low-energy particles or other quantum systems. CERN's result pushes the phenomenon into a dramatically different regime.Z bosons are massive particles, and the collisions at the LHC occur at extraordinarily high energies. The observation therefore gives physicists another way to study quantum mechanics in conditions that are difficult to reproduce anywhere else.The ATLAS and CMS collaborations had previously investigated entanglement in other short-lived particles. Researchers had observed quantum entanglement involving top quarks, which are the heaviest known fundamental particles. The Z-boson result extends such studies to massive vector bosons and provides another opportunity to examine how quantum mechanics operates at the electroweak scale.The significance of the result goes beyond confirming that quantum mechanics continues to behave strangely.Because the Z boson is directly involved in the weak nuclear force, studying its quantum properties could provide new information about how fundamental interactions work at high energies. The Higgs boson is particularly useful in this context because its decay can create pairs of Z bosons whose quantum correlations can be reconstructed.Scientists now expect much larger datasets to make such measurements increasingly precise. CERN says the future High-Luminosity LHC, or HiLumi LHC, will dramatically increase the number of collisions available for study, potentially allowing researchers to investigate quantum entanglement and other quantum phenomena at even higher energies and with greater statistical precision.For Einstein, entanglement was one of the features that made quantum mechanics appear deeply counterintuitive. At CERN, scientists are now studying that same strange behaviour not with thought experiments, but through the fleeting traces left by some of the most energetic particle collisions humans can create.The Z bosons exist for only an instant. Yet in that tiny window, their quantum states can retain correlations that offer physicists another glimpse into the rules governing the subatomic world.
Article Summary: Physicists working with the ATLAS and CMS experiments at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider (LHC) have found strong evidence that two extremely short-lived, massive particles known as Z bosons can become quantum-entangled. The result provides a new demonstration that quantum correlations can survive even at the extreme energies produced in particle collisions.Quantum entanglement occurs when two quantum systems share a linked state.

Article Title: In 1910, Oregon planted European beachgrass to stabilize shifting dunes; it spread along the coast, reshaped the landscape and squeezed open sandy habitat used by native wildlife
Article Text:
European beachgrass (Ammophila arenaria) is now well established in the Oregon dunes

How beachgrass changed the dunes

Native species lost open sandy habitat

A natural process made faster

Efforts to control the invasive grass

In 1910, Oregon introduced European beachgrass near Coos Bay to stabilise its shifting dunes. The plant trapped moving sand and helped hold the dunes in place as it was meant to. But as the beachgrass spread, it changed the coastal landscape and reduced the open, shifting sand habitats that native plants and animals had adapted to.European beachgrass (Ammophila arenaria) is now well established in the Oregon dunes and dominates large parts of the dune system. A government data on invasive plants in the Lower Coos Watershed says the species has significantly changed the local landscape. It also notes that American beachgrass (Ammophila breviligulata), which was intentionally planted near the mouth of the Columbia River in the 1930s, later spread south.The two beachgrass species have created a nearly continuous barrier from the foredunes inland towards Highway 101, changing what was once a dynamic dune system. Aerial photographs of the Oregon dunes showed that vegetation covered about 20% of the dunes in 1939. About 50 years later, more than 80% of the dunes in the same region were covered by vegetation.Earlier, Oregon’s coastal dunes were naturally shaped by moving sand.The dunes included open areas and valleys that shifted with seasonal winds. Native species such as pink sand verbena, Wolf’s evening primrose, silvery phacelia and the endangered Western Snowy Plover were adapted to these changing conditions. The introduction and spread of beachgrasses changed those conditions.European beachgrass is well adapted to seasonal sand burial. It can tolerate being buried by up to 1 metre of sand each year. This allows it to survive in conditions in which many other plants cannot.The grass also spreads through rhizomes, which are underground stems or rootstock. Pieces of these rhizomes can be carried along the shore by winter storms. Once beachgrass becomes established, it is very difficult to control and even harder to eradicate.As the grass grows, it captures and stabilises sand. This changes the movement of sand across the dune system. The establishment of non-native beachgrasses reduced the sand supply reaching interior dune habitats and changed the orientation of valleys within the Oregon dune field.Before the spread of beachgrass, the beaches associated with the Oregon dunes did not have a continuous foredune running parallel to the ocean. Instead, dunes and their valleys were oriented at an angle to the shore and shifted as prevailing winds changed with the seasons.The Coos Bay dune field, stretching from Haceta Head in the north to Cape Arago in the south, contains world's only oblique-ridge dunes. These dunes are expected to disappear as non-native beachgrass continues to stabilise the landscape.The changes to the dunes have affected species that depend on open, shifting sand. Oregon government material says populations of native plants and animals adapted to the dynamic dune system have declined sharply since beachgrass was introduced.These include pink sand verbena, Wolf’s evening primrose and silvery phacelia. The endangered Western Snowy Plover also depends on open dune habitat.Beachgrass does more than replace native plants. By trapping sand and stabilising the dunes, it reduces the open areas these species need. With less sand movement and more vegetation, parts of the dunes have become increasingly stable.The decline of native dune species is linked to changes in dune valleys and reduced sand reaching the interior dunes. These changes followed the spread of non-native beachgrasses.The government source Dune stabilisation and rejuvenation have occurred naturally over thousands of years. Research suggests that vegetation can naturally stabilise dunes, allowing a foredune to develop. Major natural disturbances can later remove that foredune and expose interior dunes to wind-driven sand movement again.These disturbances can include major events such as a subduction zone earthquake, tsunami or sea-level rise. The research suggests that non-native beachgrasses may be accelerating a natural cycle rather than creating a completely new process.However, the result is still a major change in the current dune landscape. A 1993 draft environmental impact statement cited in the source projected that the unique open dunes could completely disappear by 2040. It said reversing the process would require removing the foredune, which was considered too expensive.Because established beachgrass is difficult to remove, controlling it requires active management. Oregon’s State Wildlife Action Plan recommends mechanical and chemical treatment in priority areas, including Western Snowy Plover nesting areas and places near pink sand verbena populations.The plan also recommends controlling other invasive plants that can take advantage of stabilised dunes. These include hybrid beachgrasses, Scotch broom and gorse. Shore pine and other woody plants can also move into areas where dunes have become more stable.
Article Summary: European beachgrass (Ammophila arenaria) is now well established in the Oregon dunes and dominates large parts of the dune system. Once beachgrass becomes established, it is very difficult to control and even harder to eradicate. Native species such as pink sand verbena, Wolf’s evening primrose, silvery phacelia and the endangered Western Snowy Plover were adapted to these changing conditions.

Article Title: 'Broke into house, forced them into vehicles': Imran Khan’s son alleges aunts, cousins 'abducted' in Pakistan

Pakistani Police has already arrested ex-PM Imran Khan's sister in Lahore ahead of party's planned march. (Reuters photo)

More relatives allegedly detained

Aleema's detention ahead of PTI march

Days before Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf's planned September 27 protest march, former prime minister Imran Khan 's son Kasim Khan has alleged that several members of his extended family have been detained and that their whereabouts have not been disclosed.In a series of posts on X, Kasim alleged that his aunts Dr Uzma and Noreen, along with cousins Shershah and Shahrez, were taken from their homes after authorities allegedly entered the properties and forced them into vehicles. The claims could not be independently verified.“This is a disgrace. Now my Aunts Dr. Uzma and Noureen, along with my cousins Shershah and Shahrez have now been abducted as well,” Kasim said.“They have broken into my aunties and cousins houses and forced them into vehicles with no explanation. No reasons for arrest have been stated. No news has been released as to where they have been taken,” he alleged.Kasim described the alleged detentions as “criminal behaviour” and called for international attention to the matter.Kasim later said the two children of Shahrez, aged four and six, had initially been missing. Meanwhile, two more of my cousins have been arrested. Azeem and Sakeenah. No reasons given. No location given,” he said.The allegations follow the detention of Imran Khan's sister Aleema Khan in Lahore on Sunday. Article Summary: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf's planned September 27 protest march. Imran Khan's son Kasim Khan has alleged that several members of his extended family have been detained and that their whereabouts have not been disclosed. The allegations follow the detention of Imran Khan's sister Aleema Khan on Sunday.

Article Title: Ohio flash-flood threat persists as tornado warning ends
Article Text:
Vehicle in Ohio drives through floodwater at intersection. (Photo: Muskingam County Engineer's Office via Anadolu Agency via Reuters)

Storm warning carries 97kmph gusts

Up to 8.9cm rain recorded

A flash-flood warning remained in force across parts of southeastern Ohio into Monday morning after a tornado warning was cancelled late Sunday as severe weather continued across the region.At 11.13pm local time, the National Weather Service (NWS) issued a severe thunderstorm warning for eastern Vinton County and parts of southwestern Athens, northwestern Meigs, northeastern Gallia and northeastern Jackson counties. Radar indicated wind gusts of about 97kmph, while forecasters said a tornado remained possible.One minute later, the NWS cancelled the tornado warning for east-central Vinton and west-central Athens counties after the storm weakened below severe limits and no longer appeared likely to generate a tornado.The earlier tornado alert followed the detection of a severe storm near McArthur in Vinton County. Creola and Zaleski were among the communities that forecasters said could be affected as the storm moved east at about 24kmph.The flash-flood warning covered northeastern Vinton County, southwestern Athens County and northwestern Meigs County and was due to remain in effect until 6.30am Monday.Radar and automated gauges indicated that 6.4cm to 8.9cm of rain had already fallen, with another 2.5cm to 7.6cm possible.McArthur, Albany, Zaleski, Carpenter, Radcliffe and Creola were among the communities covered by the warning.The NWS advised people inside sturdy buildings to use a basement or an interior room on the lowest floor and stay away from windows. People outdoors, in vehicles or mobile homes were advised to seek substantial shelter, while drivers were warned not to enter flooded roads.This version removes the main repetition while keeping the latest-first structure, preserving the chronology and giving each subhead a clear factual purpose.
Article Summary: Severe thunderstorm warning issued for eastern Vinton County and parts of southwestern Athens, northwestern Meigs, northeastern Gallia and northeastern Jackson counties. Radar indicated wind gusts of about 97kmph, while forecasters said a tornado remained possible. Flash-flood warning remained in force until 6.30am Monday.

Article Title: In 2021, a sealed Super Mario Bros. cartridge bought in 1986 sold for $660,000; months later, a different sealed copy reached $2 million in a private Rally sale
Article Text:
