Another Mario cartridge reached $2 million

Super Mario Bros.

Super Mario Bros.

Super Mario Bros.

A copy ofwas bought as a Christmas present in late 1986 and spent 35 years at the bottom of an office desk drawer before its owner finally sold it for $660,000 in April 2021. The sealed Nintendo Entertainment System game became the most expensive video game ever sold at auction at the time, and a few months later, a different sealed copy ofchanged hands privately for $2 million, which pushed the value of unopened Nintendo games into a different category altogether. Heritage Auctions recorded the $660,000 auction sale, while the later $2 million transaction was handled through Rally rather than a conventional auction.The $660,000 cartridge had been purchased in late 1986 as a Christmas gift. The buyer never opened it and put it away in a desk drawer, where it remained untouched for about 35 years. The owner eventually decided to sell, with the cartridge still factory sealed. Heritage graded the game WATA 9.6 A+ and identified it as acopy from a short production period, which had the perforated cardboard hangtab packaging and a particular code configuration that placed it within a limited production run.Heritage said that this particular version was produced in late 1986 and was among the early copies to use plastic shrink wrap rather than the earlier sticker-sealed packaging. Nintendo had moved to another packaging variation by early 1987. The cartridge was unopened after decades in storage, and its packaging corresponded to a relatively short production window. Heritage described it as the oldest factory-sealedcopy it had offered at that point.Heritage sold the cartridge on April 4, 2021, for $660,000, and the amount included the buyer's premium and more than quadrupled the previous record for agame, which Heritage had set at $114,000 in July 2020. In July, a sealed copy ofsold for $870,000 at Heritage, followed two days later by a sealedthat reached $1.56 million. Thatsale became the first public video-game auction to cross the $1 million mark.The games were no longer being valued simply as old entertainment software, since condition, packaging variations, grading and provenance had become central to the collector market. The owner of the $660,000had bought it as a Christmas gift that disappeared into a desk drawer and remained there for decades. Its eventual value was determined only after collectors began paying large sums for professionally graded, unopened games.The $2 million figure that is often associated with the 2021record belonged to a different copy. Rally is a platform that allowed investors to buy fractional interests in collectibles, and it acquired its sealedcartridge for $140,000 in 2020. The company then offered shares in the game to investors, and in August 2021, those investors approved a $2 million buyout from an anonymous collector.Artnet reported that Rally had sold 3,000 shares in the game for $50 each, and the eventual $2 million transaction therefore represented a major increase over the $140,000 that Rally had paid to acquire it. However, this was not an auction unlike the $660,000 Heritage transaction, which matters because the two sales are often blended together when the 2021 video-game market is discussed. The $660,000 cartridge was bought in 1986 and sold at auction, and the $2 million cartridge was sold through Rally's fractional-ownership model.The $2 million mark eventually remained the benchmark for asale until 2026, when Heritage sold a different sealed copy for $3 million. That later cartridge was the highest-graded copy of an early sealed edition and became the new record for the game.
Article Summary: The $660,000 cartridge had been purchased in late 1986 as a Christmas gift. The buyer never opened it and put it away in a desk drawer, where it remained untouched for about 35 years. The owner eventually decided to sell, with the cartridge still factory sealed. In July, a sealed copy ofsold for $870,000 at Heritage, followed two days later by a sealedthat reached $1.56 million.

Article Title: In 2023, a charity shelter found gold Nike Air Jordans in a donation bin; the one-of-four-or-five pair sold for $50,800
Article Text:
In December, Sotheby's sold the pair for $50,800, with the hammer price going to the Portland Rescue Mission | instagram/@zimkicks

In December, Sotheby's sold the pair for $50,800, with the hammer price going to the Portland Rescue Mission | instagram/@zimkicks

The shoes looked like ordinary donations at first

BlacKkKlansman

Staff initially thought the shoes might be fake

The shoes were a custom version of the Air Jordan 3 that were designed for Spike Lee | Wikimedia Commons

The estimate was nowhere near the final price

A pair of bright gold Nike Air Jordan 3s was sitting near the bottom of a clothing donation bin at the Portland Rescue Mission in Oregon when James Free, who was a participant in the shelter's transitional program, spotted them in April 2023. He set them aside for staff to inspect, and they turned out to be custom sneakers that were made for filmmaker Spike Lee and his inner circle, one of only four or five pairs produced. In December, Sotheby's sold the pair for $50,800, with the hammer price going to the Portland Rescue Mission.The Portland Rescue Mission receives large quantities of donated clothing and shoes, which are sorted and distributed to people who need them. When Free came across the gold Jordans, their condition stood out, as they were brand new while many of the surrounding donations were used clothing and footwear.The shoes were a custom version of the Air Jordan 3 that was designed for Lee. Sotheby's described the pair as having metallic gold leather, black, white and icy-blue details, a red interior, and custom logos that were connected to Lee's production company, 40 Acres and a Mule Filmworks.The model first became publicly recognizable when Lee wore a pair at the 2019 Academy Awards. He was wearing the gold Jordans when he accepted the Oscar for adapted screenplay for. The shoes found in Portland were not Lee's personal pair, as Sotheby's identified them as one of a small number of pairs made for Lee to give to people in his circle. The model was never released to the general public.Portland Rescue Mission staff first had to determine whether the shoes were genuine. Erin Holcomb, the charity's director of staff ministry, said that the shoes initially appeared too unusual to be authentic. Staff searched for information about the model and eventually took the pair to a local sneaker business for examination, and found that the shoes were identified as genuine. Nike designer Tinker Hatfield, whose name appears on the shoes alongside Lee's, was then contacted. Hatfield authenticated the sneakers and became involved in preparing the auction lot.Nobody at the charity knew who had placed the shoes in the donation chute or why, which left the organization with a rare collector item that had arrived in exactly the same way as thousands of ordinary shoes and clothes.Hatfield also supplied material connected to the original design, and provided a replacement shoe box and signed additional material for the auction. Sotheby's included that material with the shoes, along with provenance from the Portland Rescue Mission.Sotheby's initially estimated the pair at $15,000 to $20,000, and the auction closed on December 18, 2023, and the winning price reached $50,800. The final figure was more than twice the top end of the estimate, and the entire hammer price was designated for the Portland Rescue Mission. Sotheby's waived its seller's fee for the charity, although the auction house retained the buyer's and overhead premiums.The Guardian reported that the shoes were one of only four to five pairs custom-made for Lee and his inner circle, and also confirmed that the pair had been found in the Portland shelter's donation chute in April before being auctioned at Sotheby's in December. The donor's identity was still unknown after the sale, while the $50,800 hammer price went back to the organization that had received the anonymous donation.
Article Summary: A pair of bright gold Nike Air Jordan 3s was sitting near the bottom of a clothing donation bin at the Portland Rescue Mission in Oregon. They turned out to be custom sneakers that were made for filmmaker Spike Lee and his inner circle, one of only four or five pairs produced. In December, Sotheby's sold the pair for $50,800, with the hammer price going to the charity.

Article Title: Kentucky man won $167.3 million Powerball jackpot in 2025; now arrested for fifth time after being found intoxicated in Walmart car park
Article Text:
Police found Kentucky Powerball winner asleep in a running Mustang

How James Farthing won Kentucky's record Powerball prize

Florida arrest came shortly after the jackpot win

February arrest involved an intimidation charge

Burglary and marijuana charges followed in March

July domestic violence case involved strangulation allegations

Fifth arrest adds to Farthing's legal cases

James Farthing, a Kentucky man who won a $167.3 million Powerball jackpot in April 2025, has been arrested for the fifth time since claiming the prize. The latest arrest took place on September 20, 2026, after deputies reportedly found him asleep inside a running Ford Mustang in a Walmart car park in Georgetown. Authorities charged him with being intoxicated in a public place following reports of alcohol-related impairment. The incident adds to a series of legal cases involving Farthing since his jackpot win. He had shared the historic prize with his mother, Linda Grizzle, after purchasing a $2 ticket from a Georgetown retailer.Earlier incidents included an April 2025 arrest in Florida, where Farthing was accused of kicking a sheriff’s deputy during an altercation. He later pleaded guilty to misdemeanor battery and obstruction or resisting arrest. In February 2026, he faced an intimidation charge, followed by burglary and marijuana-possession charges in March after being accused of entering a Lexington home and stealing $12,000. In July, he was arrested on domestic violence-related charges, including first-degree strangulation and fourth-degree assault. Farthing has pleaded not guilty to the domestic violence charges.The latest incident began shortly before 3 a.m. on Sunday, September 20, when a caller reported a white Ford Mustang stopped in the middle of an intersection in Georgetown, Kentucky. The vehicle later moved to a Walmart car park on Osborne Way, according to the arrest citation reported by WKYT.Deputies arrived and found the Mustang parked near an electric vehicle charging station with its engine running. Farthing was reportedly asleep in the passenger seat. Officers knocked on the window several times before he woke up.The arrest citation described several signs of impairment, including the smell of alcohol and marijuana, bloodshot and watery eyes, slurred speech and difficulty maintaining balance. Farthing was subsequently charged with being intoxicated in a public place and taken to the Scott County Detention Center.According to the arrest report, Farthing told deputies that a woman had driven him to the car park and left him there. Authorities reviewed surveillance footage, which reportedly showed no one exiting the Mustang after it entered the car park.Farthing purchased the winning Powerball ticket from Clark's Pump N Shop in Georgetown. The ticket matched the required numbers in the April 26, 2025 drawing, resulting in a $167.3 million jackpot.The Kentucky Lottery identified the prize as the largest Powerball jackpot ever won in the state. Farthing and his mother, Linda Grizzle, claimed the winnings together and announced that they would share the fortune.The win brought significant attention to the family, while Farthing later appeared in news reports concerning several encounters with law enforcement in Kentucky and Florida.Farthing's first reported arrest after winning the lottery took place in Florida in April 2025. Authorities accused him of battery involving a law enforcement officer and resisting arrest following an incident at a hotel.According to the Associated Press, officers said Farthing kicked a deputy in the face during an altercation and attempted to flee. He faced charges connected to the confrontation.The Independent later reported that Farthing pleaded guilty in the case and received a sentence of time served and $1,000 in fines.In February 2026, Farthing was arrested in Georgetown on a charge involving intimidation of a participant in a legal process. The case followed a report from a woman who contacted emergency services and said she feared for her safety.According to People, police investigated an incident at Farthing's home and reportedly found a woman hiding under a desk. Authorities also searched the property and allegedly discovered a handgun, ammunition, marijuana and drug paraphernalia.Farthing faced additional charges in March 2026 in connection with allegations of burglary and marijuana possession. Authorities accused him of entering a Lexington home and stealing approximately $12,000 in cash.The Guardian reported that investigators used security camera footage during the investigation. Farthing was later reportedly located at a casino.Local news reports said the burglary and marijuana charges were dismissed in May. The dismissal applied to those specific charges and did not resolve his other legal cases.In late July 2026, Farthing was charged with first-degree strangulation and fourth-degree assault following a reported domestic violence incident in Scott County.Police said a woman reported that a verbal argument became physical after a boating trip. According to the arrest report, she alleged that Farthing placed both hands around her neck and restricted her breathing. Authorities also reported visible marks on her neck.Farthing pleaded not guilty through his legal representative. A judge set his bond at $15,000 and ordered him to avoid contact with the alleged victim. He was also required to wear an electronic monitoring device with a notification feature.The September arrest is the fifth reported arrest involving Farthing since he won the Kentucky Powerball jackpot in 2025.The latest case concerns public intoxication in Scott County and follows the July domestic violence-related arrest. His legal proceedings remain separate from the lottery win, which he shared with his mother.The public intoxication case is pending in Scott County District Court, with an arraignment reportedly scheduled for Tuesday, September 22, 2026.
Article Summary: James Farthing won a $167.3 million Powerball jackpot in April 2025. He has been arrested for the fifth time since claiming the prize. The latest arrest took place on September 20, 2026, after deputies reportedly found him asleep inside a running Ford Mustang in a Walmart car park in Georgetown. Authorities charged him with being intoxicated in a public place following reports of alcohol- related impairment.

Article Title: In 1988, Ohio attorney Neil McKown secretly bought 155 neglected acres; 38 years later, the family farms nearly 500 acres and he declined a $400,000-$500,000 timber cut to keep the woods
Article Text:
In 1988, Ohio attorney Neil McKown secretly bought 155 neglected acres (Image Credit: Farm Progress/ Jennifer Kiel)

A secret purchase that changed the family’s future

The desire to spend more time outdoors eventually led Neil McKown to the 155-acre property in 1988 (Image Credit: McKown family via Farm Progress)

From neglected acreage to working farm

The operation steadily expanded

Image Credit: Farm Progress/Jennifer Kiel

Conservation is built into the farming system

The farm has become an outdoor classroom

A family operation moving into its next generation

A long-term view of the land

What began as a secret land purchase has grown into a nearly 500-acre family farm built around conservation, forestry and a long-term commitment to the land. In 1988, Ohio attorney Neil McKown quietly purchased 155 acres without first telling his wife, Pamela. The property was overgrown, rundown and neglected, but what initially looked like a risky decision eventually became the foundation of a nearly 500-acre family farming operation. In a report based on interviews with the McKown family, Farm Progress detailed how the family transformed the land while maintaining its woods, improving drainage and adopting conservation practices. Their efforts have now earned the family the Ohio Conservation Farm Family Award. Most notably, McKown turned down an estimated $400,000 to $500,000 timber harvest because he preferred to keep the forest standing.McKown’s first step into farming was far from conventional. After practising law with his father, he wanted an escape from the pressures of legal work and the constant demands of computers, phones and clients. He had grown up in a small farming community about five miles from the property and had worked summer jobs on farms and at an agricultural fertiliser plant.The desire to spend more time outdoors eventually led him to the 155-acre property in 1988. McKown signed the purchase agreement without telling Pamela. He waited until he returned home before revealing what he had done. After dinner, he told his family to get into the car so they could see what they had bought.The first impression was not particularly promising. Pamela described the house and property as an eyesore, while much of the land was overgrown and neglected. Still, the family decided to take on the challenge.The McKowns began with only about 80 tillable acres, leaving the remainder as woods and pasture. Neil's first attempt at growing soybeans in 1990 even prompted three neighbouring farmers to stop by and examine his grain drill, apparently concerned about his lack of farming experience. Nevertheless, the family continued. They worked on the woods during winter, removing grapevines and undertaking timber-stand improvements with assistance from conservation cost-sharing programmes. The children, Sam and Lauren, were involved in the work while they were still young.The farm also presented a significant drainage challenge. Located in a prehistoric lake basin with sandy and silty soils, the property had only one inadequate drainage outlet and a few old drainage tiles. Working with a neighbouring farmer, the McKowns developed a drainage solution that connected their property to an existing system. They subsequently tiled the farmland systematically over five years and installed 30-foot buffer strips along the ditch.The original 155 acres eventually became part of a much larger operation. The family added cattle and hay equipment in the mid-1990s, while their son Sam became increasingly involved in the agricultural work. By the time he was 14, Sam had started doing custom hay work for local farmers. He continued the work through high school and college before eventually making farming his full-time livelihood.The family's biggest expansion came when they purchased a neighbouring 220-acre farm. The operation now covers nearly 500 acres, with crops and livestock forming part of the diversified agricultural system. The farm produces corn, soybeans, wheat, hay and alfalfa, while cattle are also raised. Highly erodible areas have been converted to pasture and managed through rotational grazing.As the farm grew, the McKowns continued incorporating conservation practices rather than treating land protection as separate from agricultural production. They use vertical tillage in autumn followed by no-till planting in spring. The family also works with an agronomist and carries out grid soil sampling every three years to guide fertiliser applications. Their forestry management is particularly important to the family. They work with a professional forester and use selective harvesting to improve the condition of the woodland rather than treating the trees simply as a source of income. That philosophy became clear when the forester estimated that a more extensive timber cut could generate between $400,000 and $500,000. McKown declined, saying he would rather see the woods than cash in on the timber. The family has also removed invasive burning bush from the woodland and maintains an apiary and pond on the property.The McKowns have also used the property to introduce children to farming and natural ecosystems. Students from St. Mary’s and fifth-graders from Auburn and Shelby have visited for farm days. The family uses the property to teach about its agricultural history, glaciers and vernal pools. A naturalist from Gorman Nature Center has helped students understand the importance of the property's vernal pool, including its role in supporting salamanders and frogs.For the McKowns, the land has consequently become more than a place for producing crops and livestock. It has also become a setting where younger generations can learn about agriculture, conservation and the natural history of the region.Today, Sam is a central part of the operation, managing much of the hay production. About 90% of the hay is sold to horse owners and cattle operations, while he also raises around 15 head of beef cattle. He has expanded his own agricultural holdings by purchasing 130 acres near Ontario, Ohio, where he grows alfalfa and row crops. Forty acres there are enrolled in a 15-year Conservation Reserve Program reforestation programme. His sister Lauren pursued a different career and works for OhioHealth in Columbus, but the family's connection to the farm remains central to the story of its development.The McKowns' transformation of the property has taken nearly four decades. What started with an unexpected 155-acre purchase has developed into a nearly 500-acre farming operation recognised for its conservation practices. For Neil, the land represents something that extends beyond its immediate economic value. His decision to preserve the woods despite the potential for a $400,000-$500,000 timber harvest reflects the family's broader approach: improving the land while maintaining the natural features that make it valuable.The Ohio Conservation Farm Family Award recognises the family's conservation efforts alongside its agricultural work. And after 38 years, what McKown once described as his "pipe dream" has become a family enterprise in which farming, conservation, forestry and education continue side by side.
Article Summary: In 1988, Ohio attorney Neil McKown secretly bought 155 neglected acres. The property was overgrown, rundown and neglected, but became the foundation of a nearly 500-acre family farming operation. Farm Progress detailed how the family transformed the land while maintaining its woods, improving drainage and adopting conservation practices.

Article Title: Tesla faces trial over ‘rampant racism’ against Black workers at US plant
Article Text:
California agency's lawsuit accusing Tesla of allowing rampant race discrimination.

Racist graffiti and alleged abuse

State alleges unequal treatment

Tesla denies allegations

Former employees testify

A lawsuit accusing Tesla of allowing widespread racial discrimination at its California factory went to trial on Monday, with the state alleging that Black workers faced racial slurs, harassment, unequal treatment and limited opportunities for promotion.The case centres on Tesla's Fremont factory, the electric carmaker's flagship plant in California. The state's Civil Rights Department brought the lawsuit in 2022, alleging that the company failed to address repeated complaints about racism and violated California's Fair Employment and Housing Act.The bench trial, being heard without a jury, could continue until the end of October. Judge Peter Borkon will decide the case.Opening the state's case, lawyer Brett Watson showed the court photographs of graffiti found inside the Fremont plant. The images included the N-word, references to the Ku Klux Klan, a Confederate flag, a white supremacist symbol and messages telling Black workers to "go back to Africa".According to court documents, such material was found in areas including bathrooms, lockers, workplace benches and lunch tables.Watson also described incidents in which Black employees said they were subjected to racial abuse. One worker alleged that he was asked, "You want to hang from a tree?""Despite what Tesla might argue, you will hear Black workers were deeply offended," Watson said. "These experiences cannot be dismissed as a few bad apples … hundreds of complaints to Tesla and [the Civil Rights Department] will show these experiences were not isolated."The state alleges that racism persisted for years and that Black workers themselves used terms such as "slaveship", "the plantation" and "The Elon Slave Labor Association" to describe their experience at the factory.One Black employee told state lawyers that he heard racial slurs between 50 and 100 times a day, according to the case presented by the state.The lawsuit claims that Black employees at the Fremont plant were concentrated in lower-level jobs, received lower pay and fewer promotions, and were more frequently dismissed than white workers.The state is seeking financial compensation as well as court orders that could require Tesla to change its workplace policies and practices.The case is significant because it is the first lawsuit brought against Tesla by a government agency on behalf of multiple workers to reach trial. Unlike individual employees, the state is not bound by Tesla's employee arbitration agreements.Tesla has rejected the allegations and described the lawsuit as "misguided". The company said it has disciplined and dismissed employees for misconduct, including racial harassment and the use of slurs.It also said its Fremont workforce is majority-minority and that the plant provides "the best paying jobs in the automotive industry" to tens of thousands of Californians.Tesla lawyer Tyree Jones strongly challenged the state's interpretation of racial language during his opening statement. He repeatedly used the N-word while arguing that Black people can use the term among themselves without it being intended as a racial insult."What's up my [N-word], my [N-word] …," Jones said, adding that "none of which is used as a racial slur.""By this action, the state of California attacks the way many Black people greet each other," Jones said. "It's offensive."Jones also argued that Tesla itself had become the target of unfair treatment by the state."The most prolific employer of California is on trial and under attack by the state," Jones said.Regarding the racist graffiti cited by the state, he added, "The state is blaming the employer, when it's the victim."After the opening statements, California called three former Black Tesla employees as witnesses.One, who worked at the company from 2021 to 2024, said he was repeatedly bullied because of his race. He alleged that another employee called him the N-word, but claimed Tesla reprimanded him rather than the person who allegedly used the slur.Another witness, a former senior security manager who spent six years at Tesla, told the court that he regularly worked with human resources on discrimination complaints and had personally observed what he considered different treatment of Black employees.He also described an incident involving white employees who were allegedly found drinking alcohol at the workplace. According to his testimony, Elon Musk intervened and instructed management to override company policy and not dismiss the employees. Tesla has denied wrongdoing. The trial is expected to run through October.
Article Summary: California agency's lawsuit accusing Tesla of allowing rampant race discrimination. The case centres on Tesla's Fremont factory, the electric carmaker's flagship plant in California. The bench trial, being heard without a jury, could continue until the end of October. Tesla has rejected the allegations and described the lawsuit as "misguided"

Article Title: A woman paid just $15 for an unusual necklace at a Brooklyn flea market; years later she learned it was an Alexander Calder work, and the forgotten piece sold at Christie’s for $267,750
Article Text:
Photo credit: Christies.com

How a flea-market find becomes museum-quality art

The Christie’s sale and where the necklace fit

Why Calder’s jewellery matters

From personal adornment to auction headline

What the sale says about the market

The wider life of Calder’s wearable art

A woman, named Norma Ifill from Philadelphia, paid just $15 for an unusual necklace at a Brooklyn flea market, wore it for years without knowing its origin, and only later learned it was a work by Alexander Calder, according to a report by The Sun. The forgotten piece, a silver wire and cord necklace made around 1940, was consigned to Christie’s and sold in the auction house’s First Open sale of Post-War and Contemporary Art in 2013 for $267,750, including buyer’s premium. Christie’s results show the necklace, catalogued as “Untitled (Necklace),” achieved the high end of its $200,000 to $300,000 estimate, turning a thrift-store find into one of the standout stories of the sale. Read on to know more about this surprising incident here:The necklace’s journey began at a Brooklyn flea market, where the seller picked it up for $15 simply because she liked the way it looked. For years it remained a personal accessory, worn without any thought of its potential value or pedigree. Years later, when Ifill visited an Alexander Calder jewellery exhibition at the Philadelphia Museum of Art and had it viewed by jewellery experts, they confirmed to her that it was indeed a long-lost piece by Calder, as per HuffPost. Only later did she discover that the piece was not a generic vintage item but a work by Alexander Calder, the American artist best known for his mobiles and stabiles but also a prolific creator of wearable art.“I can’t believe I had a Calder necklace all this time and had no idea... I wore it about four-five times max and every time I wore it, people always admired it," Ifill had told Bloomberg earlier.Calder began making jewellery in the 1920s and 1930s, often crafting pieces from wire, sheet metal and found objects. He made many of these works as gifts for friends, fellow artists and dancers, and they circulated informally through social circles rather than through galleries. Over time, some of these necklaces, bracelets and brooches have been recognised as legitimate extensions of his sculptural practice, with the same playful sense of line, balance and movement that defines his larger works.The necklace appeared in Christie’s First Open sale of Post-War and Contemporary Art, a two-day auction in New York held on September 26 and 27, 2013. The sale was designed to bring together works by established names and emerging artists at accessible price points, with many lots estimated in the tens or low hundreds of thousands of dollars. In total, 281 of 399 lots offered were sold, generating $13.67 million and an 84 percent sell-through rate by value.Lot 107 in the sale was described as “Alexander Calder (1898–1976), Untitled (Necklace), silver wire and cord, executed circa 1940.” It carried a pre-sale estimate of $200,000 to $300,000. When the hammer fell, the final price, including buyer’s premium, was $267,750, placing it among the top results for jewellery and small-scale works at the auction. The buyer was recorded as European Trade, suggesting the piece was acquired by a dealer or gallery acting on behalf of a collector.Calder’s jewellery has long fascinated scholars and collectors because it blurs the line between functional object and sculpture. He often made pieces by hand, bending and twisting wire with pliers in ways that echo the construction of his mobiles. Many of the necklaces are abstract, relying on loops, spirals and open forms that move with the wearer’s body. In that sense, they are kinetic sculptures in miniature, designed to be experienced in motion rather than viewed statically on a pedestal.Art historians see these works as part of Calder’s broader experimentation with line and space. Just as his large-scale mobiles respond to air currents in a gallery, his necklaces respond to the movements of the person wearing them. That connection between art and everyday life was central to Calder’s practice and helps explain why his jewellery has gained recognition and value in the secondary market, even though it was originally made outside the traditional gallery system.For the original flea-market buyer, the necklace’s transformation from $15 accessory to six-figure artwork is a reminder of how much knowledge and context can change the meaning of an object. Worn for years as a simple piece of jewellery, it carried no special status until its attribution was confirmed. Once identified as a Calder, it moved from the realm of personal style into the world of post-war and contemporary art, where provenance and authorship drive value.The story also highlights how auction houses like Christie’s have become key players in shaping the market for artists’ jewellery. By including the necklace in a major Post-War and Contemporary Art sale alongside paintings, photographs and sculptures by names like Andreas Gursky, Keith Haring and Kerry James Marshall, the auction house positioned it as a serious work of art rather than a decorative curiosity. The strong result, near the middle of the estimate range, suggests that collectors are willing to pay significant sums for authenticated examples of Calder’s wearable art.The First Open sale results, as summarised by Christie’s specialist Saara Pritchard, showed strong demand for both rising stars and established figures. Works by artists such as Tauba Auerbach and Oscar Murillo sold above their estimates, while rare vintage pieces by Alfred Jensen, Alexander Calder and Howard Hodgkin attracted competitive bidding. The overall total of $13.67 million was the highest ever achieved for a First Open sale of Post-War and Contemporary Art at Christie’s in New York at that time.Within that context, the Calder necklace stood out not only for its price but for its narrative. A flea-market find that turned into a $267,750 sale is the kind of story that captures public attention and reinforces the idea that important works can still surface in unexpected places. For dealers, collectors and curators, it is a reminder to look closely at objects that might seem ordinary at first glance, especially when they bear the hallmarks of an artist known for working across media.Since that 2013 sale, Calder’s jewellery has continued to appear in exhibitions, publications and auctions. Museums have shown his necklaces and brooches alongside his sculptures, emphasising the continuity of his visual language across scales and materials. Private collectors have built specialised holdings of his wearable pieces, treating them as small, intimate versions of the same artistic concerns that animate his most famous public works.For the woman who once wore the necklace without knowing its origin, the Christie’s result marks a clear before and after in the object’s life. What began as a $15 purchase at a Brooklyn flea market ended as a documented, catalogued and sold work by one of the 20th century’s most celebrated artists. In the process, the necklace moved from a private story of personal style into the public record of art market history, where its new owner now holds a small but significant piece of Calder’s legacy.
Article Summary: A woman, named Norma Ifill from Philadelphia, paid just $15 for an unusual necklace at a Brooklyn flea market. She wore it for years without knowing its origin, and only later learned it was a work by Alexander Calder. The forgotten piece, a silver wire and cord necklace made around 1940, was consigned to Christie's and sold in the auction house’s First Open sale of Post-War and Contemporary Art in 2013.

Article Title: West Dallas had too few air-quality monitors to track pollution across large areas; a Plano teen built an AI model to estimate neighborhood air quality, later reaching 60 schools and training 300 yout
Article Text:
Technology is only one part of Tan's approach. Shared Skies created a 50-page environmental justice guide in English and Spanish and distributed it to more than 60 low-income schools, reaching approximately 30,000 students.

A problem close to home

Using technology to fill the gaps

Taking the message into schools

From classrooms to city councils

National recognition at 17

At 17, Nathan Tan has already taken on a problem that can be difficult even for adults to see, let alone solve: the invisible pollution hanging over neighborhoods where families have spent years carrying a disproportionate share of the environmental burden. From his home in Plano, Texas, Tan has turned concern about air quality into a growing community effort that combines technology, education and grassroots action, states a report by North Texas e-News.Tan is the founder of Shared Skies Initiative, a nonprofit focused on environmental injustice in Dallas. His work grew out of years spent tutoring elementary school students in West Dallas, where he became increasingly aware of the area's pollution problems. His own experience with respiratory illness and the loss of family members to lung cancer also gave the issue a deeply personal dimension.A student's question about why the sky looked so hazy prompted Tan to dig deeper. He found that childhood asthma rates in West Dallas are several times the Texas average, while a single air-quality monitor covers more than 900 square miles. That left many of the communities facing the greatest risks without detailed, neighborhood-level information about the air they were breathing.As per the report, Tan initially considered expanding the network of monitoring equipment, but the cost and maintenance requirements made that approach difficult to scale. Instead, he developed a machine-learning model capable of predicting particulate matter concentrations in areas without monitoring stations. Sensor data is used to validate the model, creating a real-time air-quality map that is now used by about 1,000 Texans. The project gives residents a way to track pollution in their communities without relying solely on the limited network of traditional monitoring stations, adds the report.Technology is only one part of Tan's approach. Shared Skies created a 50-page environmental justice guide in English and Spanish and distributed it to more than 60 low-income schools, reaching approximately 30,000 students. The organization has also provided 50 student-built air filters capable of reducing indoor pollution by as much as 95%, along with 10,000 KN95 masks and bilingual educational booklets. Its youth ambassador program has trained 300 young people to understand air-quality data and share practical information with their families. The effort turns students from passive recipients of environmental information into participants who can help their communities understand and respond to pollution.Tan has also taken the issue beyond classrooms and community workshops. Shared Skies has organized letter-writing campaigns and appeared before local city councils while working with grassroots organizations to bring greater attention to air-quality concerns.One focus has been a shingle manufacturing plant located just hundreds of yards from homes in West Dallas. The organization has advocated for the plant's closure and encouraged young people to participate in local discussions about environmental policy.The scale of Tan's work has now earned him national recognition. He is one of 25 recipients of the 2026 Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes, which honors young people between 8 and 18 who have made significant contributions to their communities or the environment. Fifteen of this year's winners receive $10,000 to support their service work or higher education. Tan is one of two Texas recipients this year, adds the news report.His project began with a question about hazy air and grew into an initiative combining data science, education and community organizing. At an age when most students are still deciding what direction to take, Tan has already built a project designed to give thousands of people better information about the environment around them.
Article Summary: Nathan Tan is the founder of Shared Skies Initiative, a nonprofit focused on environmental injustice in Dallas. His project began with a question about hazy air and grew into an initiative combining data science, education and community organizing. Shared Skies created a 50-page environmental justice guide in English and Spanish and distributed it to more than 60 low-income schools, reaching approximately 30,000 students.

Article Title: 'World is getting worse': Antonio Guterres warns wars, divisions are paralysing UN
Article Text:
Antonio Guterres told reporters the need for stronger oversight would be a major focus of his talks with global leaders coming to the city.

'Environment of impunity'

Wars driving food and fuel costs

UN faces pressure to reform

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has warned that the global situation is deteriorating as wars spread and become increasingly complicated, with deep divisions among major powers leaving the Security Council unable to respond effectively to growing crises.Speaking to Al Jazeera on Monday, a day before delivering his final address to the UN General Assembly as secretary-general, Guterres said the world body was facing serious challenges over its ability to deal with conflicts and uphold international law.Guterres said the involvement of major powers and permanent members of the UN Security Council in conflicts had made it harder for the council to act.He said repeated violations of international law were contributing to a broader sense that countries could act without facing consequences."That creates an environment of impunity, in which midsize powers believe that they can do whatever they want because nothing will happen to them," Guterres said.According to the UN chief, geopolitical divisions have effectively paralysed the Security Council at a time when the number of conflicts is growing.He warned that the consequences were being felt most severely by vulnerable populations caught up in wars and economic disruption.Guterres pointed to the Russia-Ukraine war and the US-Israel war on Iran as conflicts with consequences far beyond the countries directly involved.He said disruptions to food, fertiliser and energy supplies were adding to pressure on economies around the world. Problems affecting key maritime routes, including the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb, have further complicated the movement of energy and goods."The combination of the war in Ukraine with the problems of exports of foods, fertilisers, and energy through the Black Sea, if you combine it with the difficulties in the Strait of Hormuz [in the Gulf], in the Bab al-Mandeb [in the Red Sea], and in the attacks [on] oil installations in several countries of the [Middle East] region, we are creating a situation that has a devastating impact on many economies around the world," Guterres said.He said wealthier countries could eventually absorb higher interest rates and energy costs, but developing nations faced much greater difficulties.People in poorer countries, he said, were being pushed into "a desperate situation" as food and energy became more expensive and access to fertilisers became harder.Guterres, a former prime minister of Portugal and former UN high commissioner for refugees, has led the organisation since January 1, 2017.His second term ends on December 31, 2026, after which a new secretary-general will take charge.Guterres said his successor would inherit a UN facing multiple conflicts and a growing gap between the scale of global challenges and the organisation's ability to respond.He argued that reforms would be necessary if the UN is to remain an effective and relevant institution in a world increasingly divided by geopolitical rivalries.
Article Summary: Antonio Guterres says the Security Council is unable to respond effectively to growing crises. He says the involvement of major powers and permanent members of the UN Security Council in conflicts had made it harder for the council to act. He said repeated violations of international law were contributing to a broader sense that countries could act without facing consequences.

Article Title: In 1978, 13-year-old Jacob Arabo’s father gifted him a watch; years later, his creations adorned A-list wrists: ‘I had to stop being a workman’
Article Text:
Jacob Arabo’s journey from a teenager in Tashkent to Jacob & Co. founder.

From Tashkent to New York

A watch gifted by his father at 13 sparked Arabo’s lifelong fascination with timepieces.

How Jacob became ‘Jacob the Jeweler’

Arabo built his name in jewellery before turning Jacob & Co. into a luxury watch brand.

The watch that changed Jacob & Co.

From scrap gold and jewellery to elaborate timepieces, Arabo built a global luxury name.

From bling to high watchmaking

Arabo’s creations have been worn by stars including Ronaldo, Jay-Z and David Beckham.

The Astronomia moment

A family story at its heart

Poll Vote & Share your view What aspect of a watch do you value the most? Design and aesthetics Craftsmanship and quality Brand reputation 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Cristiano Ronaldo, Jay-Z, Kanye West, and David Beckham have all been photographed wearing Jacob & Co.’s now-iconic Five Time Zone watch. The brand’s name has also long been intertwined with A-listers, with a language of diamonds, gold and “bling”. But before Jacob & Co. became a name associated with elaborate timepieces, its founder Jacob Arabo was a teenager in Tashkent who had become fascinated by a watch his father gave him.He was 13 when his father, Nison, gifted him a dual-time watch. The boy was captivated by the mechanism and the idea of displaying different time zones. That childhood fascination would return decades later, when Arabo created the Five Time Zone watch. “I was fascinated by it. I think this is what led me to develop the Five Time Zone watch, that really started our watchmaking journey,” Arabo recalled in an interview with WorldTempus.Born in 1965 in Tashkent, then part of the Soviet Union, Arabo grew up in a Bukharian Jewish family. His father had been involved in manufacturing and distributing liquor, but after the family moved to the US in 1979, he struggled to find work and support the family.Arabo eventually left high school at 17 to help his family financially. “My father was an educated man… But at the time under the Soviet regime, there weren’t many opportunities to have a better life. So, in 1979, he decided to bring our family (from Tashkent, Uzbekistan) to America,” Arabo told Revolution Watch. “He found that his prospects were a lot more limited. He tried really hard to find work. But he really had trouble making ends meet, and so, at 17, I dropped out of high school to help support my family. ”The teenager then enrolled in a jewellery-making course. It was meant to last six months; he completed it in four. He went on to work in a jewellery factory, but the repetitive nature of the job soon pushed him towards designing his own pieces.“I was always curious about design,” he said, explaining that he wondered why two objects made from the same materials could look so different. He also became interested in photography and the role of perspective, detail and lighting in making something beautiful.Then came a small opportunity that changed the direction of his life. At the factory, Arabo noticed leftover gold tubing being discarded as scrap. He turned it into a bracelet- and it sold well. “I soon realized that to really support my family, I had to stop being a workman and start being a jeweler myself,” he said.Still only 17, he opened his own factory near New York’s Diamond District. He would spend four days working on designs and the remaining three visiting department stores to sell them. By 1986, at 21, he had opened his own jewellery shop on Sixth Avenue.It took years before Arabo developed a following among New York’s hip-hop community.His jewellery was different from the conventional designs of the time: larger, more conspicuous and created around the tastes of a new generation of artists who were beginning to command both cultural and financial influence.The late rapper The Notorious B.I.G. eventually gave him the name that would stick- “Jacob the Jeweler”. Arabo's work and name then began appearing in hip-hop culture, including references in songs by Jay-Z, 50 Cent, Beyoncé, Big Sean, Rick Ross, A$AP Ferg and Kanye West.Arabo had a simple explanation for why artists kept coming back. “The reason I think they all came to me was, firstly, I always treated them with respect. As a young person, I genuinely admired what they did. I admired their success,” he said. He also wanted to create what they wanted, but with the best craftsmanship and stones he could provide. That relationship between Arabo and the music world would eventually help take Jacob & Co. far beyond New York’s Diamond District.In 2002, Arabo launched the Five Time Zone watch- a design that combined the bold, gem-set aesthetic associated with his jewellery with multiple time displays.The watch quickly became a fixture in celebrity and hip-hop culture. Jay-Z, Kanye West, Busta Rhymes, Nigo, Pharrell Williams, Bono, David Beckham and Leonardo DiCaprio were among those photographed wearing it, according to Revolution Watch. Later, A$AP Rocky, A$AP Ferg, Romeo Beckham and Drake were also spotted wearing versions of the watch.But there was an interesting contradiction at the heart of its success: the original Five Time Zone was quartz-driven. For Arabo, the popularity of the watch was not the end of his watchmaking ambitions. It was the beginning.“When I get interested in a subject, I love to do research, I love to learn,” he said. He began studying traditional complications and high watchmaking and spent increasing amounts of time in Switzerland.In 2007, Arabo introduced the Quenttin, his first major venture into high watchmaking. The watch featured seven mainspring barrels and a vertical tourbillon. Its design reflected Arabo’s growing interest in making watches that were not simply decorative, but technically ambitious.The Quenttin also taught him what he wanted from future creations. “I wanted to make these kinds of super complications but in a way that was personally meaningful to me,” he said. “Even if I was to work with the best high complications specialists, the movements had to be exclusive to me.”That ambition led to the Epic SF24 in 2013, inspired partly by the split-flap information boards Arabo remembered seeing at airports and railway stations as a child. The watch displayed 24 cities and their corresponding time zones. But the watch that most clearly announced Arabo's new direction was the Astronomia, unveiled in 2014.Arabo wanted the Astronomia to look unlike a conventional watch. He imagined something connected to space, three-dimensional and open enough for the wearer to see the movement from different angles.“I knew that watches were evolving, and I wanted to create something that was totally unique. I wanted something related to space, something that was completely three-dimensional and something with a case that was totally open so that you could see the movement from every angle,” he said.The resulting Astronomia featured a rotating four-arm carriage, a triple-axis tourbillon, a floating time display, a 288-facet diamond and a miniature globe. Arabo described the experience of wearing it as “visual poetry”.It represented a striking shift: the man who had become famous for creating the watches and jewellery loved by hip-hop stars was now pursuing increasingly complex mechanical watchmaking.And yet, the two sides of his career were not as disconnected as they might appear.Arabo has said that he wanted Jacob & Co. to create watches that were visually spectacular while retaining authenticity in their watchmaking. “While I wanted to make the wildest, most ambitious watches possible,” he said, “it was important to me that from a watchmaking perspective, we always retained our authenticity in our approach.”For all the celebrity names associated with Jacob & Co., Arabo's own story keeps returning to family. His son Benjamin Arabov became CEO of Jacob & Co. in 2021. In an interview with Revolution Watch, Benjamin recalled his father as someone who made time for his sons and spoke enthusiastically about watches at home.Arabo, too, has spoken about family as one of his greatest rewards. “To me, this is the greatest reward in life- to have a family that still enjoys spending time together so much,” he said.There is, then, a quiet symmetry to Arabo's journey. The story that began with a teenage boy studying the watch his father had given him eventually became one of the world's most recognisable luxury watch and jewellery names.The celebrities may have helped put Jacob & Co. on the global stage. But long before the red carpets, music videos and elaborate mechanical creations, there was a young immigrant in New York trying to support his family- and a boy in Tashkent who simply wanted to understand what made a watch tick.
Article Summary: Jacob Arabo is the founder of luxury watch brand Jacob & Co. His creations have been worn by stars including Cristiano Ronaldo, Jay-Z and David Beckham. Arabo was inspired by a dual-time watch his father gave him when he was 13. He left high school at 17 to help his family financially.

Article Title: In 2012, Holly the Florida house cat fled after fireworks, survived a 190-mile journey and was reunited with her owners 62 days later
Article Text:
PC: ABC news

Florida cat Holly disappeared after fireworks

Holly was found weak after 62 days

Holly was found just one mile from home

Indoor cat Holly travelled 190 miles home

A house cat named Holly disappeared during a Florida holiday in late 2012 after fireworks frightened her and she bolted from her owners' motor home. Jacob and Bonnie Richter had travelled with Holly to the Daytona International Speedway, about 190 miles from their home in West Palm Beach. The family searched for the missing cat and distributed flyers before eventually returning home without her. Sixty-two days later, Holly was found in a Palm Beach Gardens garden, emaciated and weak. A veterinarian scanned her for a microchip, leading to her owners being contacted. The indoor cat had made her way back towards home.The Richters had taken Holly with them on their road trip when she became separated from them. The ABC News report said she was "spooked by fireworks" and bolted from the motor home, leaving her owners searching for her in the area around Daytona International Speedway.The family continued looking for Holly before they had to leave without her. They handed out flyers and contacted local agencies during their search, but the cat could not be found at the time. The Richters eventually returned to their home in West Palm Beach without knowing what had happened to her.Sixty-two days later, a woman named Barb Mazzola found an emaciated cat in her yard in Palm Beach Gardens. According to ABC News, the cat was "so skinny, all bones and weak" and could "hardly walk". Mazzola bought food for the animal and took her to a veterinarian on a Saturday.At the veterinary clinic, Holly was scanned for a microchip. The identification allowed the veterinarian to establish who the cat belonged to, leading to the Richters receiving a call informing them that Holly had been found.The Richters were shocked to learn that Holly had survived and made her way back to the area where they lived. According to the ABC News report, she was found only one mile from the family's home in West Palm Beach.Jacob Richter described the journey to ABC News affiliate WPBF-TV as "quite a journey for this little girl". He added: "We just can't believe she came home." The discovery meant that Holly had returned to the vicinity of her home after disappearing during the family's trip to Daytona.Holly's return was particularly notable because she was an indoor cat and had travelled a long distance after becoming separated from her owners. Veterinarian Marty Becker told ABC News that animals have a sense of direction, but said it was unusual for cats to find their way home over long distances."All animals have a sense of direction," Becker said, according to the ABC News report, adding that it was "really unusual for cats to find a way home over long distances". Holly had covered the roughly 190 miles between Daytona and the Richters' home.
Article Summary: Holly was found in a Palm Beach Gardens garden, emaciated and weak. A veterinarian scanned her for a microchip, leading to her owners being contacted. Jacob and Bonnie Richter had travelled with Holly to the Daytona International Speedway, about 190 miles from their home.

Article Title: 'Illegally entered': ICE agent shoots Venezuelan man in Texas- watch
Article Text:
ICE agent shot and wounded Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan man, in Austin, Texas. (X- @noeliaizarza)

Perez disputes account of shooting

A Venezuelan national shot and wounded by a US immigration agent in Texas was transferred to an ICE detention centre with the bullet still lodged in his body, his lawyer said Monday.Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, said he was delivering a DoorDash order in Austin on Sunday when an ICE agent allegedly rammed his vehicle and shot him."I'm in a lot of pain because the shot fractured my clavicle and at the hospital where they took me they couldn't remove the bullet because it's close to the spinal cord...I'm not doing very well, I still have the bullet inside," Perez told reporters by phone.The shooting is the latest instance of violence involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents enforcing President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, AFP reported.Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said on X that Perez had "illegally entered our country under the Biden administration and had a final order of removal". His attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, disputed that account, saying Perez was in the US legally with a work permit.Lincoln-Goldfinch said Perez was transferred from a hospital to an ICE detention centre in Pearsall, about 135 miles (215 km) southwest of Austin."He was shot here in his back, and they didn't take the bullet out, and they didn't give him pain medication, and they transferred him to ICE, to a processing center where he spent the night without a bed," she said.Perez said a truck pulled up alongside his vehicle while he was on his way to deliver the order and tried to hit him without using lights or sirens.He said a black pickup then cut him off and an agent got out and demanded his documents. Perez said he asked to pull over from the middle of the road but the agents refused."I made a U-turn and that's when he started chasing me, thinking I was going to run away, but I was looking for a place to leave my car safely," he said."That's when he hit me twice and shot me."Perez said he did not know how many shots were fired.After the shooting, an ambulance took him to hospital, where he said doctors initially ran tests in preparation for surgery to remove the bullet. He alleged that the procedure was later halted because agents were in a hurry to discharge him and transfer him to detention.Lincoln-Goldfinch alleged that there was "absolutely zero justification" for the shooting and called for an end to ICE traffic stops.
Article Summary: Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, said he was delivering a DoorDash order in Austin on Sunday when an ICE agent allegedly rammed his vehicle and shot him. The shooting is the latest instance of violence involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents enforcing President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown.

Article Title: James Monroe's 1,200-acre Virginia estate is finally becoming a state park after years of efforts to protect the former president's home
Article Text:
PC: The Conservation Fund

Oak Hill preserves more than James Monroe's presidential history

PC: AP News

Virginia lawmakers push Oak Hill towards state park status

A 1,200-acre estate was protected ahead of public ownership

More than 10,000 people joined the campaign for Oak Hill

Oak Hill's history extends beyond James Monroe

Oak Hill becomes Virginia's newest state park

For years, Oak Hill Farm sat in southern Loudoun County as a privately held piece of Virginia history, its fields and woodland surrounding the former home of President James Monroe. The estate is now set for a different future. According to The Conservation Fund, in July 2026, Virginia lawmakers approved the acquisition of more than 1,200 acres at Oak Hill, clearing the way for the property to become the state's newest state park. The decision follows years of efforts by lawmakers, conservation groups and local residents to protect the land. It also places Monroe's former home within a larger public landscape that carries stories reaching beyond the fifth US president, including those of enslaved people and Indigenous communities connected to the area.Oak Hill lies near Aldie, south of Leesburg, between James Monroe Highway, Little River Turnpike and Tail Race Road. The property contains farmland, forest and the house associated with Monroe, making it one of the remaining privately owned properties tied directly to a US founding-era president.Monroe lived at Oak Hill during the later part of his life. The estate is therefore connected to a period that followed his presidency, rather than simply serving as a site linked to his years in Washington.Its significance, however, is not limited to the person who owned it. The land also preserves evidence of the people who worked and lived there, including enslaved people, as well as the longer Indigenous history of the surrounding landscape.The move towards state park status did not happen in a single legislative session. As reported by America’s State Parks, Del. John McAuliff, who represents parts of Fauquier and Loudoun counties, introduced House Bill 500 during Virginia's 2026 legislative session with the goal of securing the property for public ownership.Reportedly, the bill passed the House unanimously, 98-0. It was later carried forward into the 2027 legislative session, but the process changed when Gov. Abigail Spanberger included the Oak Hill acquisition in a budget amendment.The Virginia legislature voted to accept that amendment in July, completing the state's approval of the purchase.McAuliff had made preservation of Oak Hill one of his priorities during his first term. State Sen. Russet Perry, who represents parts of Loudoun and Fauquier counties, had also worked towards state park designation since taking office in 2024.Their efforts were part of a broader campaign involving local supporters and conservation organisations.The Conservation Fund became a central part of the preservation effort before the state formally approved the park.Reportedly, the organisation purchased Oak Hill in November 2025, protecting the estate while arrangements for its eventual transfer to public ownership continued. That step kept the 1,200-plus acres together rather than allowing the historic property and surrounding land to face an uncertain future under private ownership.The fund's involvement also reflected the scale of the site. Oak Hill is not simply a historic house and a small surrounding garden. Its landscape stretches across farmland and forest, creating a substantial tract of open land in addition to the presidential connection.The eventual state park will therefore combine historic preservation with public access to a much larger landscape.The campaign to preserve Oak Hill attracted support from well beyond the politicians directly involved. According to The Conservation Fund, more than 10,000 people supported the acquisition through petitions, letters and personal donations. That response helped demonstrate local and wider interest in keeping the property intact and securing public access.Heather Richards, the fund's Mid-Atlantic vice president, said the level of public involvement was unusually strong for one of the organisation's preservation projects.The campaign also brought together state officials, conservation advocates and members of the local community. The approval was presented by those involved as a bipartisan effort, with both Democratic legislators and the governor playing roles in moving the project forward.Turning Oak Hill into a state park will make the property accessible as public land, but its historical story extends well beyond Monroe's ownership.The estate's past includes the people who maintained the farm and household during an era when slavery was part of Virginia's social and economic system. The surrounding area also has Indigenous histories that predate Monroe and the establishment of the United States.Those layers are likely to shape how visitors understand the site. The house can tell the story of a former president, while the wider estate provides a setting for examining the people and communities whose lives were tied to the property.The acquisition adds more than 1,200 acres of farm and forest to Virginia's public estate and establishes Oak Hill as the state's newest state park. It also places Monroe's former home within a system designed to preserve historic and natural resources while allowing people to visit and use the land.The timing is closely tied to the 250th anniversary of American independence in 2026. State officials and supporters have pointed to the anniversary as an appropriate moment to secure the property for long-term public ownership.The transition does not erase the years of uncertainty that preceded it. Oak Hill reached state park status only after repeated legislative efforts, conservation work and a public campaign to keep the estate together.Now the property has a different status. What was once a privately held presidential estate is being preserved as public land, with its house, fields and forests set to remain part of Virginia's landscape for generations to come.
Article Summary: Oak Hill Farm in southern Loudoun County, Virginia, is a 1,200-acre estate. It is the former home of President James Monroe, who lived there during the later part of his life. More than 10,000 people joined the campaign to protect the land. In July 2026, Virginia lawmakers approved the acquisition of more than 1, 200 acres at Oak Hill, clearing the way for the property to become the state's newest park.

Article Title: Northeast US airports resume operations after telecom outage disrupts thousands of flights
Article Text:
The disruption was linked to two equipment failures. (Reuters photo)

What caused the disruption

Newark sees hundreds of diversions

A second failure made matters worse

US airports across the Northeast began returning to normal on Monday after a telecommunications failure disrupted air traffic operations at several major airports, causing more than 1,000 flight delays and cancellations.US transportation secretary Sean Duffy said the communications lines had been repaired and operations were gradually resuming, although passengers were still expected to face delays as airlines worked through the backlog."The telecom lines have been repaired, and all airport operations in the Northeast are resuming," Duffy said.The disruption began at around 10 am after a circuit failure at the Federal Aviation Administration's Philadelphia Terminal Radar Approach Control facility knocked out radio and radar equipment used to manage aircraft around several airports.The failure affected New York's John F Kennedy International Airport, LaGuardia Airport and Newark Liberty International Airport, as well as Philadelphia, Teterboro and Westchester County airports.The outage meant that flights headed for some of the airports could not land and were instead held at their departure points or diverted to other airports.Flightradar24 said JFK and LaGuardia were added to the list of airports where departing flights were being held because of the FAA equipment failure.Newark, Teterboro, Philadelphia and Westchester County were also affected.Newark saw particularly heavy disruption. Flightradar24 said arrivals resumed at the airport later in the day after a prolonged halt."Arrivals have just resumed at Newark. No commercial flights landed at EWR between 09:38 and 17:22 local time today," Flightradar24 posted.By 5.30 pm local time, 107 flights had been diverted from Newark to 34 different airports, affecting 25 airlines, according to the flight-tracking service.Washington's Dulles International Airport received 19 of those diverted flights, while JFK took 12. United Airlines, which operates a major hub at Newark, was the airline most affected, with 70 diversions.The disruption was compounded when officials discovered that a newly installed fibre-optic backup system in New Jersey had also been damaged during construction work.Duffy said a fibre-optic line near an Amtrak railway line had been cut, affecting Verizon communication lines.FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the incident exposed weaknesses in the agency's existing infrastructure and called for changes to the network design."The network design is terrible. And if we don’t fix the network design, we’re going to continue having these failures," he said.The disruption came as New York prepared to host world leaders and ministers for the 81st United Nations General Assembly, adding to the importance of restoring normal airport operations.By around 6 pm, Duffy said the telecommunications lines had been repaired and airport operations across the Northeast were resuming. However, passengers were warned that delays could continue as airlines cleared the disruption's knock-on effects.
Article Summary: More than 1,000 flight delays and cancellations across the Northeast. Flights headed for some of the airports could not land and were instead held at their departure points or diverted to other airports. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the incident exposed weaknesses in the agency's existing infrastructure.

Article Title: Pakistan in crisis: PTI to hold Sept 27 stir 'at all costs'; Imran Khan's sisters challenge detention orders
Article Text:
Pakistan: Imran Khan's sisters challenge detention orders in court, demand immediate release

PTI says September 27 protest will go ahead

Family condemns detentions

Pakistan's opposition Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) will proceed with its planned September 27 protest demanding the release of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan, even as legal challenges have been filed against the preventive detention of his three sisters.A petition was filed in the Lahore High Court on Monday challenging the 30-day detention orders issued against Aleema Khan, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, according to a report by Pakistan-based daily The Express Tribune, as cited by news agency ANI.The petition, filed by Shahraiz Khan, son of Aleema Khan, seeks to have the detention orders declared invalid and the immediate release of the three women.The detention orders were issued by the Lahore deputy commissioner on September 20 under Section 3 of the Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, ahead of PTI's planned September 27 demonstrations.Aleema Khan was detained earlier, while Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi were detained on Monday.The petition alleged that Aleema Khan was intercepted while travelling for personal errands and that there was no public gathering or situation at the time that could pose a threat to public order. It also stated that Aleema Khan and her driver, Muhammad Ameer, were being held at Lahore Central Jail.The petitioner described Aleema Khan as a law-abiding individual and alleged that the detention order did not contain specific allegations justifying preventive detention.The respondents named in the petition include the home department secretary, Lahore deputy commissioner, capital city police officer and Lahore Central Jail superintendent, according to The Express Tribune.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister Sohail Afridi said on Monday that PTI would go ahead with its September 27 protest “at all costs”. He said the party would announce its detailed protest plan on September 25 and mobilise workers across Pakistan.Afridi said arrests of PTI provincial ministers and lawmakers had begun ahead of the protest, prompting an emergency meeting of the party's parliamentary group.He said the party had pursued “all constitutional and democratic avenues” but was being prevented from meeting Imran Khan despite court orders.Afridi said PTI had no intention of confrontation and would pursue its demands through peaceful and democratic means. He also said party workers would not carry weapons during the protest.PTI chairman Barrister Gohar said the party was not planning to “storm” Islamabad and would not take the law and order situation into its own hands. He said the authorities were provoking the party but PTI would not come to Islamabad “like terrorists”.Interior minister Mohsin Naqvi, meanwhile, said the government would not allow the September 27 protest to disrupt Islamabad. Speaking to reporters in Lahore on Monday, he said preparations were under way for an “assault” and that the government would not allow the capital to be shut down.Imran Khan's son, Kasim Khan, also condemned the detention of his relatives and appealed for international intervention.In a post on X, he said, “This is a disgrace. Now my Aunts Dr Uzma and Noreen, along with my cousins Shershah and Shahrez, have now been abducted as well. They have broken into my aunties' and cousins' houses and forced them into vehicles with no explanation. No reasons for arrest have been stated.”He added, “No news has been released as to where they have been taken. This is criminal behaviour. Inexcusable. The Pakistani people are petrified of their own leaders. No upstanding nation should tolerate this criminal establishment. Intervention is now imperative. The world MUST take action.”The arrests come as PTI prepares for the September 27 protest seeking the release of Imran Khan, who has been in jail since 2023 and is currently held at Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi.
Article Summary: A petition was filed in the Lahore High Court on Monday challenging the 30-day detention orders issued against Aleema Khan, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi. The petition, filed by Shahraiz Khan, seeks to have the detention orders declared invalid and the immediate release of the three women. Imran Khan's son Kasim Khan also condemned the detention of his relatives and appealed for international intervention.

Article Title: 'PTI's drama will never achieve anything': Pak minister Naqvi warns Imran Khan's party ahead of Islamabad march
Article Text:
Mohsin Naqvi warns Imran Khan's PTI

Also Read:

(With agency inputs)

Pakistan interior minister Mohsin Naqvi on Monday warned jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) ahead of the party’s planned protest in Islamabad, saying it “can never achieve anything through such drama. "The PTI plans to march towards the capital on September 27 to demand the release of its founder Imran Khan, who has been in jail since 2023 after being arrested following his conviction in a corruption case. Currently, the cricketer-turned-politician is lodged at the high-security Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi.“We will not allow PTI to enter Islamabad and shut down the city for several days. We have clearly told them that they can never achieve anything through such drama, and I will say again that there is still time; they should not go into this situation,” Naqvi told reporters.He also referred to an Islamabad high court order directing the federal government to ensure peace in the capital and claimed that a majority of PTI leaders did not support the planned protest.“Do not harm yourself and your workers,” he told the PTI leadership, urging it to adopt a “different approach”.Asked about measures to find a long-term solution to the PTI’s repeated protests, Naqvi replied, “This time we will find a permanent solution; we will not leave it halfway.We can't afford this every time.”On reports of a possible ban on the party, he said the government would seek a “once-and-for-all solution.”Meanwhile, the federal government was stepping up security measures ahead of the protest, including placing shipping containers along roads and bringing in police personnel from other provinces.More than 22,000 security personnel, led by eight senior police officers, were to be deployed in Islamabad, while more than 30,000 were to be stationed in Attock district, which connects Khyber Pakhtunkhwa with Punjab.Police in Rawalpindi, Islamabad’s twin city, have separately sought 9,000 additional personnel to assist the local administration.The PTI is not the only group planning protests in Islamabad. Right-wing Jamaat-e-Islami launched a demonstration against rising petroleum prices on Sunday and was heading towards the capital from Karachi.The Kissan Ittehad farmers’ group has also announced a sit-in in the city this week, seeking relief for farmers.
Article Summary: Mohsin Naqvi warns Imran Khan's PTI ahead of planned protest in Islamabad. Interior minister says party "can never achieve anything through such drama" Federal government stepping up security measures ahead of the protest. More than 22,000 security personnel, led by eight senior police officers, to be deployed.

Article Title: Pakistan airstrikes on Afghanistan: 3 killed, several injured as conflict fears grow
Article Text:
Relations between Kabul and Islamabad have remained strained over militant activity along border. (AP photo/ File)

Taliban warns of 'crushing response'

Kabul denies sheltering TTP

Afghanistan keeps door open for talks

Poll Vote & Share your view What should be the main focus for Pakistan and Afghanistan in resolving their issues? Diplomatic negotiations Border security Intelligence sharing Ceasing cross-border operations 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

At least three people were killed and several others injured in a Pakistani airstrike targeting Afghanistan's northeastern Kunar province, Tolo News reported on Monday, citing a provincial official.The military strike is supposedly in retaliation for suicide bombing at a police station compound in northwestern Pakistan, raising fears that tensions between the neighbouring nations could once again turn into open fighting.Pakistan and Afghanistan were involved in their most serious military confrontation in years in February.
